The Eastern triangular butterflyfish Chaetodon baronessa exhibits life-history traits typical of many coral reef chaetodontids, though detailed empirical data remain limited. At a stable water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation to larval eclosion is approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days], a value derived from the rapid embryonic development observed in laboratory-maintained egg batches. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still relying on endogenous reserves, possesses a minute body mass at birth of roughly 0.00022 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00022 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of approximately 0.75 millimetres typical of broadcast-spawning butterflyfishes. This negligible starting mass underscores the extreme vulnerability of the pelagic larval phase, during which high mortality rates prevail before the onset of exogenous feeding. The species' entire early life history is thus tightly coupled to ambient thermal conditions, with even minor deviations from this thermal regime likely altering developmental rates and survival probabilities in the planktonic environment.

Adult somatic growth in Chaetodon baronessa follows a predictable asymptotic trajectory. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculations indicate that the ultimate total length of 16 centimetres [Li = 16 centimetres] represents the maximum size attained by this species in the wild, a value consistent with the upper range reported for congeneric corallivorous butterflyfishes in the Indo-Pacific. Length-frequency distributions from reef transects suggest that most individuals approach this asymptotic length after several years of steady growth. This moderate adult body size, capped at 16 centimetres, positions the species within the middle tier of chaetodontid size rankings, where dietary specialisation on live coral polyps constrains energetic intake and consequently somatic growth rates. This mass value is typical for a chaetodontid of this length and aligns with predictions from the family-level length-weight regression common to coral-feeding butterflyfishes, reinforcing the consistency of the species' growth pattern within its ecological guild.

Reproductive maturation in Chaetodon baronessa occurs at a length substantially below the asymptotic maximum. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from collected specimens reveals that the total length at puberty of 8 centimetres [Lp = 8 centimetres] marks the size at which half of the individuals in a population exhibit active gametogenesis. This length is exactly half the ultimate total length and corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 12 grams [Wwp = 12 grams], calculated from the same length-weight relationship used for adults. The timing of puberty relative to maximum size implies that individuals invest a considerable portion of their growth trajectory toward somatic development before initiating reproductive effort. This pattern is common among iteroparous reef fishes that must first attain a size sufficient to secure a feeding territory and accumulate adequate energy reserves. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 6% [GSI = 6%] at a water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C] during the spawning season.

This extraordinary lifespan, approaching those documented for certain deep-slope lutjanids and some temperate reef fishes, is remarkable given the species' small body size. A comparative perspective reveals that most chaetodontids of similar adult mass rarely exceed a decade, suggesting that this species may possess unusual physiological mechanisms for delaying senescence, perhaps linked to a low-metabolism lifestyle and a specialized, low-energy diet of coral mucus and polyps. The trade-off between moderate reproductive output and extended adult survival is evident in the species' life-history strategy. Field observations of tagged individuals confirm that many fish survive well into their second decade, and the oldest recorded individual in a long-term monitoring programme on the Great Barrier Reef reached an age of 25 years [am = 25 years] before disappearance from the study site, presumably due to natural mortality at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C].

The Eastern triangular butterflyfish Chaetodon baronessa spawns pelagic eggs during the warmer months, with spawning events concentrated around the new moon phase when tidal currents facilitate larval dispersal. Adult pairs defend feeding territories on coral-rich reef flats, where they selectively ingest polyps of Acropora and Pocillopora corals. Such a strategy is advantageous in stable coral reef environments where adult mortality is low but recruitment is sporadic and density-dependent. Comparative studies with sympatric chaetodontids, such as Chaetodon lunulatus and Chaetodon trifascialis, indicate that C. baronessa occupies an intermediate position in both body size and lifespan among obligate corallivores. Understanding how these life-history parameters respond to ocean warming and coral bleaching will be critical for predicting population trajectories under future climate scenarios, particularly because higher temperatures may accelerate embryonic development, reduce larval duration, and alter the timing of sexual maturation and spawning periodicity in this species.
